questions.stem: What is Model Evaluation in Machine Learning, and how does it help determine whether a trained model makes accurate and reliable predictions?
options: Model Evaluation measures how closely a trained model fits the records it learned from. Consistently low training error is enough to establish accurate and reliable predictions.
Model Evaluation measures how well a trained model performs using evaluation data and suitable metrics. It helps determine whether the model can make accurate predictions on unseen data.
Model Evaluation compares predictions with evaluation labels, but uses the resulting score to keep updating the model until the same evaluation data yields its highest accuracy.
Model Evaluation uses metrics collected during training to estimate reliability. Testing on new examples is unnecessary once multiple training batches have produced similar scores.

questions.stem: Why is evaluating a Machine Learning model only on its training data insufficient, and what role does unseen test data play?
options: Training data provides the strongest estimate of generalization because those examples are well understood by the model. Unseen test inputs mainly check whether file preprocessing succeeded.
A model can be evaluated on its training records if they are shuffled first. The resulting error usually reflects performance on unfamiliar data without needing an independent test set.
Training performance alone cannot show whether a model has learned useful patterns or memorized examples. Unseen test data measures how well the model generalizes to new inputs.
Using an unseen test set helps estimate generalization, but the test set should also guide feature choices and hyperparameters before the model's final accuracy is reported.

questions.stem: What are the main evaluation metrics used for classification and regression models, and how do they measure different types of prediction performance?
options: Classification uses accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score to measure prediction correctness. Regression uses MAE, MSE, and RMSE to measure differences between predicted and actual numerical values.
Classification mainly uses MAE and RMSE to count wrong class predictions, while regression uses precision and recall to judge how close numerical predictions are to targets.
Classification metrics such as recall and F1-score measure average numeric distance from actual values, while regression accuracy calculates the percentage of exactly matched outputs.
Classification uses accuracy, precision and recall to measure decisions, while regression uses MAE and MSE; RMSE measures the average absolute error without applying any square root.

questions.stem: How do precision, recall, F1-score, and confusion matrices provide a more complete evaluation of classification models than accuracy alone?
options: Precision measures the portion of actual positives that were detected, while recall measures the portion of predicted positives that are correct. F1 averages these values arithmetically.

Precision measures all correctly classified inputs, while recall measures errors on negative predictions. A confusion matrix summarizes both rates without separating false positives and false negatives.
Precision and recall measure different kinds of positive predictions, but F1-score emphasizes whichever one is larger. Confusion matrices omit true negatives because only positive classes matter.

Precision measures correct positive predictions, recall measures detected actual positives, and F1-score balances both. A confusion matrix shows true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives.

questions.stem: How do cross-validation, baseline models, and hyperparameter tuning contribute to reliable Model Evaluation and model selection?
options: Cross-validation gives repeated scores, but baselines are needed only after hyperparameter tuning. The final test set should be used to choose settings before reporting the winning model.

Cross-validation evaluates performance across multiple data splits, while baseline models provide reference scores. Hyperparameter tuning uses validation results to select settings without using the final test set.
Cross-validation estimates performance across splits, and baselines provide reference scores, but choosing hyperparameters from the highest score on the final test set improves objectivity.
Cross-validation evaluates multiple partitions, while baseline models are chosen by training accuracy. Hyperparameters should be tuned on whichever test split produces the highest performance.

questions.stem: How should Model Evaluation handle imbalanced datasets, probability calibration, and distribution shifts to avoid misleading performance results?
options: Imbalanced datasets require metrics such as precision, recall, F1-score, and PR-AUC. Calibration measures probability reliability, while distribution-shift testing checks performance when data patterns change.
For imbalanced datasets, accuracy becomes more informative as the rare class gets smaller. Calibration confirms that positive predictions are ranked correctly, even if probabilities are wrong.
On imbalanced datasets, precision and recall are useful, but probability calibration is unnecessary when F1-score is high. Distribution shift can be handled by keeping the same threshold.
PR-AUC evaluates the minority class, while calibration checks how often a model changes its predicted class. Distribution-shift testing compares training and testing set sizes, not changing patterns.

questions.stem: How can Model Evaluation frameworks prevent data leakage, ensure fair benchmark comparisons, and monitor prediction quality after model deployment?
options: Fair benchmarks are achieved by applying each model's preferred metric and test samples. Reusing test results during tuning is acceptable when every model has the same opportunities.
Leakage-free evaluation means no training labels are copied directly into test inputs. Monitoring data drift after deployment replaces the need for held-out testing before release.

Reliable evaluation uses independent test sets, consistent metrics, leakage-free validation, and standardized benchmarks. Production monitoring tracks prediction quality, data drift, and performance degradation over time.
Evaluation frameworks need independent tests and repeatable metrics, but reusing benchmark results for feature selection is safe if the team records the exact experiments for comparison.
